content: Observational studies in epidemiology involve passive observation of groups or populations without any controlled intervention. Alternatively, individuals may be classified by their immune response status and followed to compare the occurrence of clinical endpoints. For instance, Chen et al. utilized a measles outbreak among university students shortly after a blood drive to study immune responses. Most students had received the measles vaccine during childhood. Although individuals with PRN titres above 120 did not develop classical measles, 70% of those with titres below 1052 reported at least one symptom, compared to 35% of those with titres above 1052. These findings support a PRN titre of 120 as a correlate of protection against clinical measles. In another example, Jack et al. followed children vaccinated with a plasma-derived hepatitis B vaccine in The Gambia. They found that achieving a peak antibody level above 10 IU/L within a year of vaccination was associated with protection against persistent hepatitis B infection over the next seven years. Natural history studies analyze immune responses after recovery from infectious diseases to identify protective components of acquired immunity. For example, Ndumbe et al. The findings suggested that these immune responses were sufficient to protect against subsequent chickenpox, as second episodes of the disease are rare. Maternal-newborn studies provide evidence for the protective role of maternal antibodies in neonates. It revealed that infants with low pre-vaccination titres (e.g., 1:6 or 1:12) did not seroconvert after measles vaccination, highlighting the importance of maternal antibody levels in determining vaccine efficacy. Case-control studies compare immune marker levels prior to disease onset among individuals who did or did not develop the clinical outcome of interest. For example, during a randomized controlled trial (RCT) of an acellular pertussis vaccine in Sweden, stored serum samples were analyzed. Children who developed pertussis had lower pertussis toxin (PT) IgG antibody levels compared to those who did not, indicating that PT IgG levels correlate with protection. Population-level studies have also been used to investigate vaccine efficacy. For instance, the efficacy of the BCG vaccine against pulmonary tuberculosis was found to be lower in Malawi compared to the United Kingdom. Studies showed that unvaccinated adolescents in Malawi had higher baseline IFN-γ responses to tuberculosis antigens than their UK counterparts, which influenced the immune response after vaccination. The Prentice criteria, introduced in 1989, provide a framework for validating surrogate endpoints in vaccine trials. These criteria require that protection against the clinical endpoint is significantly related to vaccination, the surrogate endpoint is significantly related to vaccination, and the surrogate endpoint is significantly related to protection against the clinical endpoint. However, these criteria have limitations, as they assume a single causal pathway between vaccination and clinical protection, which may not always be the case. Alternative methods, such as the proportion of treatment effect (PTE) explained by a marker, have been proposed to address these limitations. For example, Storsaeter et al. used logistic regression to show that IgG antibodies against pertussis antigens explained 93% of the vaccine's protective effect. Similarly, the Qin framework distinguishes between correlates of risk and surrogates of protection, providing a hierarchical approach to assess immune markers. Threshold methods assume a specific immune marker level above which individuals are fully protected and below which they remain susceptible. For example, a PRN titre above 120 mIU/mL was identified as a protective threshold against measles in a study by Chen et al. These methods can also estimate vaccine efficacy by relating immune marker distributions to clinical outcomes. In summary, various study designs and statistical methods are used to identify and validate immune markers as correlates or surrogates of vaccine-induced protection. These approaches provide critical insights into vaccine efficacy and inform public health strategies.
